title: Staccato surge sandbox — microburst soak notes
content:
Objective:
Run a set of microburst / staccato arrival patterns against a small dedicated cluster to see: 1) how often cold-KV-cache penalties show up in p99, 2) whether transient batching improves or worsens p95 under tiny bursts, and 3) how admission and queueing behave when burst spacing is sub-second. Quick note: 'staccato' = very short bursts separated by variable quiet windows (mimics interactive assistant spikes).

Testbed summary:
- Cluster: 3 x A10G-equivalent nodes, each with 40GB GPU RAM, 8 vCPU worker agents
- Serving binary: runtime v2.7.1 (local build with microbatching toggle)
- Model: open-llama-13b-8bit (quantized FP16->int8-like path for throughput)
- KV cache: server-side 64k-entry LRU, per-tenant namespace, hit probe instrumentation enabled
- Traffic generator: custom Python harness (staccato-driver) that can emit Poisson+burst mixing and exact microbursts; uses persistent connections and client-side warmup to avoid TLS noise
- Measurement: internal tracing (trace_id), token-level timing, CPU/GPU utilization, queue-length histograms, batch size distributions, and tail latencies (p50/p95/p99) measured at gateway and node.

Scenarios executed (short):
1) Baseline steady qps 40 RPS (single-token prompt), 10m soak.
2) Staccato-1: 1s bursts of 200 RPS every 10s (duty 10%), keep for 15m.
3) Staccato-2: sub-second microbursts: 200 RPS for 300ms every 6s.
4) Staccato-3: randomized spacing (exp(mean=6s)) with microbursts of 150-350 RPS.
5) Cold-cache restart: same as Staccato-2 but restart servers once during run to force cold KV cache + JIT paths.

Key knobs toggled between runs:
- microbatching: on/off
- priority lanes: soft-priority vs single-lane
- prefill aggregation window: 0ms, 10ms, 25ms

Representative results (extracted aggregated summaries):
- Baseline (steady 40 RPS): p50=12ms, p95=38ms, p99=84ms, avg batch size=1.9, kv_hit=87%

- Staccato-1 (1s bursts / 10s): p50=15ms, p95=72ms, p99=320ms, avg batch size=3.4, kv_hit=82%
  Observations: p99 dominated by a small set of cold-JIT and cache-miss traces during burst ramp-up. Gateway shows queue spikes up to 60 concurrent requests at burst peaks.

- Staccato-2 (300ms bursts / 6s): p50=18ms, p95=140ms, p99=520ms, avg batch size=4.1 (but high variance), kv_hit=74%
  Observations: sub-second bursts cause batching to grow erratically — batches accumulate quickly, then drain; some requests experience extra queuing while waiting to fill a batch. Microbatching improved throughput but shifted some percentiles worse.

- Staccato-2 with prefill 10ms: p50=16ms, p95=95ms, p99=260ms, avg batch size=3.1, kv_hit=76%
  Observations: small prefill window reduced worst tails and kept batch sizes modest. 10ms hit seemed a good sweet spot for this model/hardware combo.

- Cold-cache restart run: sharp p99 spikes > 1.2s tied to first burst after restart, KV cache miss ratio jumped to 98% for first 90s, then decayed to baseline.

Resource/Counters (notes):
- GPU util: peaks 78-92% during bursts, but frequent oscillation (sawtooth) in Staccato-2.
- CPU utilization for inference workers spiked due to microbatch assembly and copy routines during microbursts.
- Memory (host): no OOM but increased GC pressure in runtime when many tiny batches queued.

Trace examples (anecdotal):
- trace_id=tr-20250221-0043: request waited 28ms in queue (prefill window=0) then batch size=7, execution=43ms, end-to-end 93ms.
- trace_id=tr-20250221-0043b: warm cache variant same burst: wait 8ms, batch=2, exec=16ms, end-to-end 30ms.

Quick conclusions:
- Microbursts sub-second are the worst offender for p99; batching that triggers too aggressively can make p95/p99 worse despite improving throughput.
- Small prefill windows (5–15ms) reduce tail risk for these patterns by limiting over-aggregation.
- KV cache warmup matters — if an application cannot tolerate the first-burst penalty, we need proactive priming or a warm shadow workload.
- Priority lanes (soft-priority) help for keeping interactive p50 low but can increase overall jitter in tail latencies unless combined with prefill caps.

Next experiments (TODOs):
- Run same scenarios with runtime v2.8 candidate that has new batching scheduler (ticket JIRA-PERF-898).
- Try adaptive prefill: start with 5ms and bump to 25ms if queue length > X (prototype in staccato-driver).
- Add client-side jitter to burst spacing to see impact of synchronization across tenants.
- Measure request-level cost delta (tokens * worker-ms) to quantify unit economics tradeoffs for microbatching vs prefill.

Open questions / loose thoughts:
- Is there a good heuristic to bound max batch size during microbursts without harming throughput? (cap + per-request timeout?)
- Could we pre-warm KV cache with light priming traffic timed shortly before expected bursts (prediction-driven)? Feels application-specific but could be offered as a managed feature.
- Explore a hybrid lane: low-latency lane with strict batch cap + background aggregated lane for best-effort throughput.

Practical notes for replication:
- staccato-driver flags used: --burst-size 200 --burst-width 0.3 --period 6 --warmup 60s --connections 400
- runtime flags: --microbatching={on,off} --prefill-window-ms={0,10,25} --priority-lanes={soft,single}
- artifacts: saved traces under /tmp/staccato/2025-02-21/, raw telemetry dumps uploaded to S3 (s3://redwood-perf/staccato-2025-02-21/).

Appendix: minimal ASCII summary table (p99 focused)

Scenario        | p50   | p95  | p99  | avg batch | kv_hit
-------------------------------------------------------
Baseline        | 12ms  | 38ms | 84ms | 1.9       | 87%
Staccato-1      | 15ms  | 72ms | 320ms| 3.4       | 82%
Staccato-2      | 18ms  |140ms | 520ms| 4.1       | 74%
Staccato-2+10ms | 16ms  |95ms  | 260ms| 3.1       | 76%
Cold-restart    | 22ms  |180ms | 1.2s | 3.5       | 12% (initial)

End notes: keep this file as a running lab notebook. If anyone wants raw traces or wants me to reproduce a specific run, ping me (ryder.chen@redwood.ai) or open JIRA-PERF-842.
